note: Single source of truth for the WMFC scan. Pages read this file. Edit here, redeploy, site updates.

Tier 1.label: Built for sector
Tier 1.def: Stated purpose is to prepare, credential, support or operate education outside district-run schools.

Tier 2.label: Names sector
Tier 2.def: Institutional text explicitly names private, classical, charter or non-traditional settings — or a dedicated school-choice course exists.

Tier 3.label: Incidental
Tier 3.def: Reaches these educators only as a side effect, or is explicitly built around district partnership.

Tier 0.label: Nothing found
Tier 0.def: No offering identified. Absence of evidence, not evidence of absence.

complete.label: Systematic pass
complete.def: Every institution in the defined population was read individually. A Tier 0 row here means nothing was found after looking for it.

partial.label: Partial pass
partial.def: Some institutions read individually, the rest covered by a summary row. State totals are incomplete by design.

placeholder.label: Placeholder
placeholder.def: One or two rows surfaced by national search rather than a state scan. Records what was found, never what exists.

Florida.note: The State University System education units, three Florida College System baccalaureate providers, and the major private institutions.

Michigan.note: All eight public universities that authorize charter schools, plus one row recording statewide authorizing context.

Ohio.note: Two private institutions read individually. The public universities are covered by one summary row and have not been read one by one.

Indiana.note: IU East surfaced in a national microschool search. Indiana has not been scanned.

Arizona.note: ASU, the University of Arizona, Northern Arizona University, Grand Canyon University and Rio Salado College read individually (October 2026). Other Maricopa colleges, Pima and the smaller private colleges have not been read. State context: Arizona funds more than 100,000 ESA students, yet its own teacher scholarship, the Arizona Teachers Academy, counts service only in public or charter schools, and about 0.7% of ESA spending reaches any postsecondary institution.

Arkansas.note: The University of Arkansas only. Arkansas has not been scanned.

West Virginia.note: One row covering both WVU and Marshall. Neither was read institution by institution.

California.note: One summary row standing for the whole state, held as a low-choice control. No institution has been read individually.

New York.note: One summary row standing for the whole state, held as a low-choice control. No institution has been read individually.

institutions.name: University of Florida
institutions.evidence: Course-level pass completed: the School of Teaching & Learning undergraduate course list was enumerated in full. Zero courses on school choice, vouchers, ESAs, homeschooling or microschools. UF also operates P.K. Yonge, a PreK-12 lab school that is a department of the College of Education.

institutions.name: Florida State University
institutions.evidence: No choice centre or credential found. FSU operates Florida State University Schools, a lab school — vehicle present, unused for this purpose.

institutions.name: University of South Florida
institutions.evidence: Homeschool-facing activity is admissions and dual enrolment only. The InED network of 125+ microschools serving 8,000+ students operates in the same metro area.

institutions.name: University of Central Florida
institutions.evidence: Center for Community Schools scales a model that structurally requires a school district as a core partner.

institutions.name: Florida International University
institutions.evidence: No education-unit choice program found. The micro-credential office sits in Student Affairs.

institutions.name: Florida Atlantic University
institutions.evidence: School Leaders Program is a formal university–district partnership whose stated aim is 'the best public education.'

institutions.name: University of North Florida
institutions.evidence: Recoded 28 October 2026 from Tier 0, under Correction 03. The graduate portfolio is conventional, which is what the July pass read. UNF’s Florida Institute of Education lists KIPP Jacksonville, a charter network, among its named school partners alongside Duval County Public Schools, and our 2026 placement survey codes UNF “open in practice” for that reason. Reach into the non-district sector exists, but as a partnership side effect, not program design.

institutions.name: Florida Gulf Coast University
institutions.evidence: The M.A. Educational Leadership P-12 non-certification track names 'teachers working in private schools, charter schools, academies or non-traditional education settings.'

institutions.name: University of West Florida
institutions.evidence: CORRECTED 8 AUGUST 2026 — was coded Tier 0. The University of West Florida appears in the Florida Department of Education's own Directory of Charter School Sponsoring Entities as an approved sponsor (entity 87), and its Board of Trustees has approved the university as authorizer of a Somerset Academy charter elementary school. Our July pass read only the School of Education program roster — CAEP-accredited through 2030, nothing choice-facing — and coded the institution Tier 0 on that basis. That was the precise error this Index exists to avoid. Our own method states that operating and authorizing moves are coded, not just programs, because a catalog scan misses the main event. We then made the catalog-scan mistake in our own home state. Recoded Tier 1 for the authorizing move. The education-unit finding is unchanged and stands alongside it: no program built for the sector was identified in the School of Education.

institutions.name: Florida A&M University
institutions.evidence: Four departments, CAEP-accredited, entirely conventional.

institutions.name: New College of Florida
institutions.evidence: No teacher preparation found despite the classical-education pivot. Standing alert if classical teacher prep launches.

institutions.name: Flagler College
institutions.evidence: Institute for Classical Education (2023–): seminars, contracted PD, summer workshop with a Classical School Leadership track. Audience overwhelmingly choice-funded. Crucially non-credit.

institutions.name: Trinity College of Florida
institutions.evidence: B.A. Elementary Education explicitly places interns in 'Christian schools, public schools, charter schools or overseas mission schools.'

institutions.name: Nova Southeastern University
institutions.evidence: THE ONLY CONFIRMED RETRENCHMENT IN THE SCAN. Nova Southeastern built a choice-sector program and no longer offers it. The evidence is the university's own: NSUWorks, NSU's institutional repository, holds a Program Overview titled “NSU Master's Degree in Charter School Education/Leadership”, attributed to the Fischler Graduate School of Education and Human Services, indexed under keywords including charter school, Miami-Dade, specialization and modified core. The current master's roster of the Abraham S. Fischler College of Education & School of Criminal Justice was read in full on 8 August 2026 (education.nova.edu/degrees/masters): Applied Behavior Analysis, Child Protection, Criminal Justice, Developmental Disabilities, Education, Educational Leadership, Leadership. No charter or choice-sector program appears. Coded Tier 0 because Tier reflects what is currently offered. The limit: the repository dates the document only as approximate (2002, deposited 2016) and it carries no discontinuation record. Existence and current absence are both documented; the date the program ended is not, and should not be asserted. Why it matters: every other Tier 0 row in this Index records an institution that has not built. This one records an institution that built and stopped. Those are different phenomena and the four competing explanations do not treat them the same way. Rechecked 28 October 2026 under Correction 03. NSU also runs a private PreK–12 school, NSU University School, which describes itself as “an academic center of Nova Southeastern University.” Its tuition page states: “NSU University School does not participate in any state scholarship, grant, or voucher programs. These programs make the school vulnerable to restrictions and reporting requirements that limit operational independence.” Source. That is the scan’s first documented case of a university operating a school outside the district system and declining portable funding on principle. Tier unchanged: the school is not built for the sector, by its own choice.

institutions.name: Palm Beach Atlantic University
institutions.evidence: Feeds Christian schools by affiliation; no program names the sector.

institutions.name: Southeastern University
institutions.evidence: FLDOE-approved early childhood degree. Affiliation, not program design.

institutions.name: Stetson University
institutions.evidence: Conventional teacher preparation; nothing surfaced across two searches.

institutions.name: University of Miami
institutions.evidence: The 'homeschool navigator' hit proved to be an advising role governing credit overloads. False positive cleared. Rechecked 28 October 2026 under Correction 03. UM has run an online private school, the University of Miami Global Academy; a 2013 report put it above 300 high school students and adding a middle school (Miami Today). Its current status could not be verified: the university’s landing page no longer loads. Tier unchanged until a current source is found. Standing alert.

institutions.name: Tallahassee State College
institutions.evidence: First Florida College System institution approved as a charter authorizer (Jan 2023), then founded Tallahassee Collegiate Academy (Aug 2023) — from outside any college of education.

institutions.name: Central Michigan University
institutions.evidence: THE MICHIGAN FINDING. College of Education & Human Services offers an online M.A. in Educational Leadership with a Charter School Leadership emphasis — program text names 'public, private, charter, and virtual schools, educational service providers, authorizers.' The first preparation program built for the choice sector found anywhere in this scan. Context: CMU became the nation's first university charter authorizer (1994) and remains its largest — the Governor John Engler Center partners with roughly 70 schools serving about 30,000 students. The authorizing center sits outside the education college; the degree sits inside it.

institutions.name: Grand Valley State University
institutions.evidence: Charter Schools Office authorizes 78 schools serving 34,000+ students. Beyond authorizing: 'Charter Through College' programs — campus visits, dedicated advising, and a Charter School Alumni Scholarship — build a student pipeline from its charter schools into the university. Institutional engagement at scale; no dedicated preparation degree found in this pass.

institutions.name: Michigan (system context)
institutions.evidence: Eight Michigan public universities and three community colleges authorize charters statewide; university authorizers may charter anywhere in the state. Michigan is the deepest university-charter ecosystem in the country. Six university authorizers remain unexamined.

institutions.name: Indiana University East
institutions.evidence: IU East High School — a microschool on campus, presented under the School of Education as 'an on-campus lab school.' Part of the Indiana Microschool Collaborative. The education unit is running a microschool.

institutions.name: Arizona State University
institutions.evidence: Arizona law lets universities under the Board of Regents sponsor charter schools, and ASU uses it: “ASU Preparatory Academy is chartered by Arizona State University” (ASU Prep). ASU Prep runs in-person and online schools, ASU Prep Digital accepts Arizona ESA funds, and ASU Prep Global runs a Microschool Entrepreneur Fellowship that helps people open microschools. All of it sits in the K–12 arm, not the education college. Rechecked 28 October 2026.

institutions.name: University of Arizona
institutions.evidence: Pathways to Teaching is built with the Sunnyside Unified School District in Tucson. UA is a lead campus for the Arizona Teachers Academy, the state’s tuition-waiver program, whose recipients must “teach in an Arizona public or charter school” for each year of support; private-school service does not count (Maricopa, JLBC). Arizona law would let UA sponsor charter schools; no UA-sponsored charter was found.

institutions.name: Northern Arizona University
institutions.evidence: Tuition-free certification pathways are built with the Tolleson and Littleton elementary districts and funded through the Arizona Teachers Academy, whose service requirement counts public and charter schools but not private ones. Arizona law would let NAU sponsor charter schools; no NAU-sponsored charter was found.

institutions.name: Grand Canyon University
institutions.evidence: One of the largest education producers in the country. Its Canyon L.E.A.P. to Teach pathway names the sector: it “may apply to teachers who hold an emergency teaching, alternative teaching or subject matter expert certificate or those who teach in a charter or private school.” Other pathways are framed around districts. False positive cleared: Grand Canyon Private Academy, an online private school that takes ESA funds, is run by Stride/K12 and has no stated tie to the university.

institutions.name: Rio Salado College
institutions.evidence: Maricopa’s online college runs dual enrollment for about 9,700 high school students through nearly 50 partner schools. In 2025, 200 of the 408 high schoolers on track for an associate degree came from one charter network, Heritage Academy. Real reach into the charter sector, through a K–12 service rather than educator preparation.

institutions.name: University of Arkansas
institutions.evidence: Department of Education Reform: Ph.D. with a dedicated parental school choice course. A research degree, facing no licensure constraint.

institutions.name: Ohio public universities
institutions.evidence: Ohio law permits university sponsorship; Bowling Green State sponsored Toledo School for the Arts. No education-unit program surfaced. Authority present, penetration high, little built.

institutions.name: University of Dayton
institutions.evidence: Ed Leadership M.S.E. prepares graduates for 'public, private, and parochial' sectors.

institutions.name: Ashland University
institutions.evidence: Operates a Homeschool and Classical Learning Center 'designed to help homeschooled and classical learning students transition into higher education.' Admissions-side engagement with the homeschool sector — the first Ohio institution found naming it. Softens, but does not overturn, Ohio's null: still no educator-preparation program.

institutions.name: WVU / Marshall University
institutions.evidence: Despite a now-universal ESA (~$5,436/student), nothing surfaced at either flagship. Low search depth — provisional, should not be used as evidence yet.

institutions.name: California institutions
institutions.evidence: Control. No ESA or voucher exists; no university program surfaced. Microschools operate privately without university involvement.

institutions.name: New York institutions
institutions.evidence: Control. No funding mechanism. Teacher U left Hunter College in 2011 and became Relay — the choice sector's pipeline exited the university and formed its own accreditor.

institutions.name: Oakland University
institutions.evidence: THE DEEPEST STRUCTURAL INTEGRATION IN THE STATE — AND STILL NO PROGRAM. The Office of Public School Academies is housed inside the School of Education and Human Services, in Pawley Hall, and reports through it. The authorizer's own text states the reason: the office's placement within SEHS “demonstrates further our commitment to excellence, marshalling the strength of its programs and faculty to increase the proficiency and expertise of Academy teachers and administrators.” Chartering policy adopted 1995; first school opened 1996; currently seven academies with over 4,800 students, deliberately capped and geographically restricted to Macomb, Oakland and Wayne counties. OU/PSA's stated vision is to “advance excellence in public education through choice.” Campus pipeline programs run across five units, plus academy-student scholarships. And yet: the SEHS Department of Organizational Leadership's M.Ed. and Ed.S. in Educational Leadership prepare candidates for building-level roles — principal, assistant principal, dean of students — with no charter, choice or non-district emphasis in the program text. Of all eight Michigan university authorizers, Oakland has bound authorizing most tightly to its education school and has built the least curriculum from it. This is the sharpest available test of whether proximity produces programs, and it comes back negative.

institutions.name: Saginaw Valley State University
institutions.evidence: A PRICE MECHANISM, NOT A CURRICULUM. The School/University Partnership Office was established by the SVSU Board of Control in 1995 and now serves over 10,000 students across 17 academies statewide; authorizer accreditation from AdvancED in 2017, renewed by Cognia through 2027. The engagement that reaches the education unit is financial: the PSA Teacher/Administrator Scholarship gives teachers and administrators of SVSU-authorized academies 50% tuition remission at 3–5 years of academy service and 75% at 6+, for up to 15 credits per year, explicitly “to obtain continuing education credits or to complete a program through the College of Education.” Coded Tier 1 because its stated purpose is to credential educators working outside district-run schools. The limit matters as much as the finding: the subsidy changes the price of the standard degree, not its content. No course, concentration or credential in the College of Education is built for the sector the scholarship recruits from.

institutions.name: Northern Michigan University
institutions.evidence: THE FLOW RUNS THE WRONG WAY. NMU resolved to authorize in 1995 and currently holds nine academies, including two centred on Native American culture (Joseph K. Lumsden Bahweting Anishnabe, Nah Tah Wahsh) and one on academic service learning (North Star). The Charter Schools Office names the education unit explicitly — but as a beneficiary, not a provider: the academies “provide an excellent opportunity for hands-on classroom experience for NMU's hundreds of elementary and secondary education majors… as they prepare for their student teaching experiences and professional careers.” Charter schools are the practicum sites; the preparation they feed is conventional licensure. The School of Education, Leadership and Public Service offers an M.A.E. in Educational Administration: Administration and Supervision with no choice-sector content identified. The institution uses the sector to train teachers for the system, not the system to train teachers for the sector.

institutions.name: Eastern Michigan University
institutions.evidence: Founded 1849 as the nation's first four-year teaching degree; the College of Education runs over 95 distinct programs. The Charter Schools Office oversees nine public school academies across Wayne, Oakland, Washtenaw, Genesee and Saginaw counties, and its own description places the education unit inside the arrangement — the office operates “with the support of Eastern's College of Education, the Michigan Department of Education, and the Michigan Association of Public School Academies.” That naming is the whole of the Tier 2 evidence. Nothing in the College of Education's catalogue answers it: Educational Leadership — K-12 Administration (M.A.), Educational Leadership (Sp.A., Ph.D.) and Curriculum & Instruction — Leadership (M.A.) are written for conventional building and district administration. The largest teacher-preparation history in the state, nine schools of its own, and no offering built for either.

institutions.name: Ferris State University
institutions.evidence: The Charter Schools Office reports through Academic Affairs, organisationally separate from the School of Education in the College of Arts, Sciences and Education — the opposite arrangement to Oakland's. Its published vision, mission and six core values concern oversight quality (academics, finances, operations, governance) and make no reference to preparing or credentialing anyone for the sector. On the education side, the M.S. in Educational Leadership is built around a sponsored internship in which candidates are “sponsored and mentored by a local district or approved educational organization” — district named first, the alternative left generic. Coded Tier 3 on that district-first framing. The authorized-schools roster was not enumerated in this pass; a third-party profile reports roughly 21 academies and 9,200 students, which is not a WMFC-verified figure and should not be cited as one.

institutions.name: Lake Superior State University
institutions.evidence: Nineteen academies on the published roster (enumerated in full, 8 August 2026), several of them explicitly non-conventional models — iCademy Global, Innocademy and Innocademy Allegan, Macomb Montessori Academy, two W-A-Y (Widening Advancements for Youth) academies. LSSU is actively expanding: an application window for new academies runs 18 May – 1 June 2026 for schools opening no earlier than 2028–29, and the office states it seeks applications offering “a unique educational option not already available in the proposed area” — an authorizer selecting for differentiation on purpose. The School of Education points the other way: its stated commitment is “preparing teachers for small, rural schools” through partnerships with districts in the Eastern Upper Peninsula and Ontario. Teacher Education (EDUC) offerings show no choice-sector content. The authorizing arm recruits novel school models; the preparation arm trains for rural districts.

institutions.name: Miami Dade College
institutions.evidence: THE INFRASTRUCTURE MOVE. Miami Dade College is an approved charter sponsor under the 2021 statutory change permitting Florida College System institutions to sponsor charters within their service area. It went considerably further than sponsoring: MDC powers the Florida Charter Institute, whose Authorizing Division reviews applications and conducts oversight on behalf of higher-education authorizers generally — including Pasco-Hernando State College. One college now operates the authorizing apparatus other colleges use. MDC's board approved its first six charter applications in February 2026. Limits: the MDC education unit has not yet been enumerated to WMFC standard, so this row codes the authorizing move only and no claim is made about MDC's teacher-preparation offerings in either direction. The institute sits outside the education unit, as at Tallahassee State College and Central Michigan University.

institutions.name: Pasco-Hernando State College
institutions.evidence: Approved by the State Board of Education to sponsor charter schools; listed in FLDOE's Directory of Charter School Sponsoring Entities as entity 86 (PHSC K12). Its stated purpose is explicit about the sector: sponsorship is “intended to offer additional, high-quality educational options for the communities located in the two PHSC service areas.” The college issued its first charter to Dayspring Academy's Early College Academy — a school that had operated for roughly a decade under the Pasco County school board, meaning the move transferred an existing school from district to college oversight rather than creating a new one. PHSC accepts applications only by RFP and partners with the Florida Charter Institute to review them. Limits: the PHSC education unit has not been enumerated to WMFC standard; this row codes the authorizing move only.

hypotheses.name: No relationship between policy and response
hypotheses.detail: High-policy states both with and without engagement; zero-policy controls with none. Not random, not simple.

hypotheses.name: Universities respond when they can hold or authorize a school
hypotheses.detail: This edition was designed to test H2 and the test came back negative. All eight Michigan public university authorizers are now coded. Six were added in August 2026 and none has a preparation program. Scale-of-holding does not rescue the hypothesis either: Grand Valley State holds 78 schools and 34,000+ students — more than Central Michigan — and has built no degree. Nor does organisational proximity: Oakland houses its authorizing office inside the School of Education and Human Services and states that the placement exists to raise the expertise of academy teachers, and its leadership degrees remain generic building-level preparation. Holding schools, holding many schools, and holding them inside the education college were each present without producing a program. H2 as stated no longer survives; whatever explains Central Michigan is more specific than the instrument.

hypotheses.name: Accreditation and licensure define what can be built
hypotheses.detail: Every form of engagement found in the six new Michigan institutions stops at the licensure boundary, without exception. Saginaw Valley State's tuition remission is for teachers and administrators of its academies — licensed roles — pursuing conventional College of Education credentials. Northern Michigan routes its academies into practicum placements for candidates seeking standard licensure. Eastern Michigan's leadership degrees are written for building and district administration. Nothing anywhere in the Index serves the unlicensed slice — microschools, homeschool co-ops, ESA vendors — which is where the 750,000 microschool students are. H3 now fits every observation in 39 institutions.

hypotheses.name: No procurement channel to individual buyers
hypotheses.status: Untested, but the Nova Southeastern case now bears on it
hypotheses.detail: Central Michigan's program is fully online and sold to individuals — mild counter-evidence that the channel is impossible. The Nova Southeastern case is now documented rather than suspected: NSU's own repository holds a Program Overview for a Master's in Charter School Education/Leadership that no longer appears on its roster. A program in this space was built and did not survive. Whether it failed for want of buyers, for want of a channel to reach them, or for reasons internal to the institution is exactly what H4 asks and what the record does not yet answer. The discontinuation is undated, so no inference about timing or cause is available.

gaps.title: The snapshot never became a series
gaps.body: Surfing the Pipeline (2023) is the only systematic catalog scan of education schools for choice-sector offerings — published the very year Florida went universal, making it a near-perfect baseline. Baselines only matter if someone takes the second reading. Nobody has.
gaps.evidence: Cheapest high-value study available in this space.

gaps.title: 'An enterprising dean' assumes the barrier is imagination
gaps.body: The 2023 recommendation locates the obstacle in vision and initiative. It never tests the alternatives: accreditation and licensure limits, or the absence of a sales channel to individual buyers. Michigan now suggests a third: time-with-the-instrument — CMU's program follows thirty years of authorizing.
gaps.evidence: Three years of universal ESA money in Florida produced zero programs.

gaps.title: Catalog scans cannot see what universities actually did
gaps.body: The method searched catalogs for programs and classes. Most confirmed university entries — running a microschool, authorizing charters, founding a school — never appear in a course catalog. The dominant institutional response is invisible to the dominant research method.
gaps.evidence: ASU Prep, IU East High School, Tallahassee Collegiate Academy and GVSU's 78 schools all return null in a catalog search.

gaps.title: Policy adoption is tracked; workforce capacity is not
gaps.body: School Choice Matters analyses all 50 states across roughly 40 policy areas — a genuinely impressive instrument for measuring whether a state has passed the policy. It contains nothing on whether the educator workforce exists to staff what the policy enables.
gaps.evidence: A state can score well on every policy dimension while having no trained supply.

gaps.title: The quality tracker covers the wrong denominator
gaps.body: The Teacher Prep Review evaluates 1,244 elementary programs across 1,053 institutions — but only 59 non-traditional programs, because traditional routes produce 96% of prepared teachers. Defensible sampling for its purpose; it also means the fastest-growing school sector sits outside the field's main quality instrument.
gaps.evidence: Standards are benchmarked to what new teachers need in conventional classrooms.

gaps.title: The sector's own association is investing in the other direction
gaps.body: Education bachelor's degrees fell from roughly 109,600 to 90,700 over two decades. The field's flagship 2026 response was a request for $2.5 billion in federal funding to rebuild the traditional pipeline — a bet on the existing model at the moment the demand side is being restructured.
gaps.evidence: No comparable investment or position addressing non-district settings surfaced.

gaps.title: Nobody has looked at the mature systems
gaps.body: The Netherlands has funded school choice constitutionally since 1917, with roughly three-quarters of primary pupils in privately-run publicly-funded schools. Sweden since 1992, Chile since 1981. England deliberately moved teacher training out of universities into schools. These are the equilibrium cases — and Michigan's thirty-year story suggests exactly why maturity matters.
gaps.evidence: US-only framing makes a century-old question look new.

gaps.title: University leadership frames this as demography, not competition
gaps.body: Declining education enrolment is absorbed into the enrolment-cliff story — US high school graduates peaked in 2025 and are projected to fall 13% through 2041. That is real. But it converts a structural shift in where students and educators go into a demographic story that implies waiting it out.
gaps.evidence: Sixteen non-profit colleges closed in 2025 and eight more in Q1 2026 — the pressure is read as demographic across the board.

gaps.title: No one owns the seam
gaps.body: EdChoice measures families, programs and fiscal effects. ExcelinEd measures policy adoption. NCTQ measures preparation quality. NACSA measures authorizers. AACTE represents the preparation pipeline. Each does its own job well. Whether the workforce exists to staff what the policy enables falls between all of them.
gaps.evidence: Every other gap on this list is a symptom of this one.

context.metric: Florida students using any choice option
Microschool operators who are licensed educators
AACTE federal ask to rebuild teacher preparation

corrections.title: We said about two in three universities showed no response. After a second search, it is about half.
corrections.detail: Our first pass searched mostly education schools. A second search on 28 October 2026, of each “none” row’s K–12, online, charter, lab-school and outreach units, recoded 17 of 70 universities. Twelve run, founded or authorize schools: among them UT Austin’s 24-campus charter district and online high school, UC San Diego’s Preuss School, USC’s Hybrid High, WashU’s sponsorship of KIPP St. Louis and Rutgers–Camden’s LEAP Academy. No response found now stands at 46% of the AAU, 55% of the Most Innovative and five of seven in Florida. We also withdrew the claim that responses sit mostly outside the education school; the recoded schools are split. Each recoded row is marked in the data. Still unresolved: UC Davis, Howard, Miami and a separate pass on district partnerships, which the first pass coded unevenly.

corrections.title: We said no university helps people start or staff a microschool. Arizona State does.
corrections.detail: The October university scan searched education schools for microschool preparation and reported 0 of 102. ASU Prep Global, Arizona State's K-12 unit, runs a Microschool Entrepreneur Fellowship that trains parents, educators and school leaders to open microschools. The headline is now 1 of 102. The program sits outside the education school. Near-miss checked and not counted: the Micro Schools Network certificate pairs Harvard's general Instructional Leadership Certificate with an MSN-written microschool course. Before coding 'none found,' K-12, online and outreach units are now searched, not only the education school. Wording narrowed 2026-10-28: the fellowship is built for founders, so the site says ASU helps people open a microschool rather than trains people to teach in one, and 'none' reads 'none found.'

corrections.title: We coded the University of West Florida Tier 0. It is a registered charter school sponsor.
corrections.detail: Our July pass read UWF's School of Education program roster, found nothing built for the portable-funding sector, and coded the institution Tier 0 — nothing found. UWF is listed in the Florida Department of Education's Directory of Charter School Sponsoring Entities as an approved sponsor, and its Board of Trustees has approved it as authorizer of a Somerset Academy charter elementary school. The row is recoded Tier 1. The error matters more than the row. This Index's central methodological claim is that catalog scans miss the main event, because universities enter this sector by operating and authorizing schools rather than by listing courses. We made exactly that mistake, in Florida, which is our most heavily covered state. It was caught by reading the state's own sponsor directory — a source we should have read in the first pass and have now added to the method.
